title: Day 68 · Week 9, Day 5 — Protocol: screening decisions as a couple — every test on one calendar, the detection rates, why a positive screen is never a diagnosis, the needle risk as it's measured now, who wants to know the sex, and a seven-line worksheet
summary: The Protocol episode that turns Days 59, 65 and 66 into a decision. The testing window opens on Day 70: carrier screening, cell-free DNA from 10 weeks, the nuchal scan and combined screen at 11–13+6 weeks, CVS at 10–13 weeks, amniocentesis from 15 weeks, the quad screen at 15–22 weeks and the anatomy scan at ~20 weeks. ACOG Practice Bulletin 226: every patient offered both screening and diagnostic testing, with the right to decline. The scoreboard for trisomy 21 (quad 81%, combined 82–87%, integrated/sequential 95–96%, cfDNA 99%; Gil 2017: 99.7% detection, 0.04% false positives across 35 studies). Why a positive screen is an instruction to get a diagnosis, not a diagnosis. The needle risk recalculated: Akolekar 2015 (0.11% amniocentesis, 0.22% CVS) and Salomon 2019 (0.30% and 0.20%, falling to 0.12% and ~0 in risk-matched studies), against the one-in-two-hundred still quoted; CEMAT 1998 and why amniocentesis waits until 15 weeks (clubfoot 1.3% vs 0.1%). The three reasons couples test, and declining as a fourth legitimate position. Fetal sex: cfDNA accuracy by week (Devaney 2011), ultrasound at 12–14 weeks (Efrat 2006), the sex-chromosome caveat, and the four disclosure arrangements.
action: Twenty minutes together before Day 70: one page, seven lines — (1) carrier screening status/result; (2) cfDNA yes/no, cost, draw week; (3) nuchal scan yes/no and booking between Day 77 and 97; (4) if high-chance, CVS or amniocentesis?; (5) the first sentence each of you would say if a diagnosis were confirmed; (6) sex: both know / neither / one / envelope, and whether sex-chromosome results are reported; (7) who gets the phone call. File it behind the Questions page of the Day 61 pregnancy file.
